query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding about 3 at.% Al to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will promote the in situ formation of a protective Al2O3 layer during high-temperature exposure, thereby significantly improving its oxygen resistance (preventing pesting) while preserving its intrinsic room-temperature ductility and high-temperature strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with inadequate oxygen resistance during high-temperature air exposure.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 3 at.% Al into the HfNbTaTiZr alloy during arc melting to create a modified alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Expose the alloy to air at 800 °C for 5 hours and test its mechanical performance (room temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength under strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1 up to 1000 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent, and dense alumina (Al2O3) scale on the alloy’s surface.
generation.mechanism: The preferential oxidation of the minor Al addition leads to the formation of a protective Al2O3 film that acts as a barrier against oxygen diffusion, thereby retarding the oxidation process (pesting) without compromising the alloy’s inherent mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-doped HfNbTaTiZr alloy will exhibit significantly reduced oxidation (lower weight gain and absence of pesting) during a 5-hour air exposure at 800 °C, while retaining room-temperature ductility in the 8–16% range and high-temperature yield strength similar to the untreated material.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance (pesting) under high-temperature air exposure despite its useful room-temperature and high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to hold under conditions of 800 °C air exposure for up to 5 hours and under mechanical loading conditions corresponding to strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1 at temperatures reaching 1000 °C.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the precise impact of 3 at.% Al on the adhesion and uniformity of the alumina scale, as well as on any potential minor changes to the alloy’s mechanical properties; further experimental verification is needed to optimize the Al content.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one set of standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and another with ~3 at.% Al added via arc melting. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, conduct surface analyses (using SEM and XRD) to investigate the oxide scale formation and measure weight gain. Additionally, perform room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature mechanical tests at 1000 °C (with strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1) on both sets.
measurements: Surface oxide composition and morphology (verification of continuous Al2O3 formation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloy does not form a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale (evidenced by porous or non-protective oxide layers) or if its mechanical properties (room-temperature ductility outside 8–16% or significantly lower yield strength at 1000 °C) deteriorate compared to the untreated alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

In the last few decades, the development of nickel-based superalloys has allowed a steady increase in operating temperatures of jet turbine engines, which leads to enhanced engine performance and efficiency. However, nowadays the engine operating temperatures have reached around 80% of the melting points of the materials, [1] i.e. , almost reaching the upper limit of usability, making it impossible to further increase the operating temperature. Thus, it is urgently needed to develop new materials that can withstand higher operating temperatures to achieve better performance, higher engine efficiency, and lower greenhouse gas emissions.

High entropy alloys (HEAs), complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), and multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are the most common names of a new group of materials [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ] introduced by Yeh et al. [ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. A new approach to HEA design using the valence electron concentration (VEC) was recently proposed with the aim of increasing the plasticity of these alloys [ [10] , [11] ]. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. decision.trend: In refractory high-entropy alloys, researchers have progressively explored how minor changes in alloy composition lead to the formation of protective phases without sacrificing mechanical performance. Early work on Hf‐based alloys (e.g., PMC10759803) demonstrated that adding a small amount of a modifying element (in that case Cr) can beneficially alter phase compositions and achieve a better balance of strength and ductility. In related systems, such as Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi alloys (PMC7299626), controlled introduction of interstitial species (oxygen or nitrogen) has been used to manipulate oxide or complex formation. Although these studies focused on mechanical behavior or damping, they indicate that composition change is an effective lever to trigger new surface phenomena (e.g., formation of dense, protective oxides) without negating the intrinsic properties of the base refractory alloy.
decision.unsolved: For equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, the critical open issue remains whether a single, minor compositional intervention can reliably form a protective oxide scale—one that prevents pesting during 5 h air exposures at 800 °C—while preserving the alloy’s as-cast room-temperature ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength. The exact protective element, its optimum concentration, and the mechanism by which it improves oxygen resistance remain untested in this equiatomic composition.
decision.lever: alloy composition (minor addition of ~3 at.% Al)
decision.why: The next plausible step follows the observed trend that controlled dopant additions can induce the formation of a stable, protective oxide scale—such as the dense Al2O3 layer—in refractory high‐entropy alloys. Leveraging the niche indication that a composition change (through a minor dopant like Al introduced via arc melting) may protect against oxidation without degrading mechanical properties, the proposed experiment would cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with approximately 3 at.% Al and then evaluate its performance under 800 °C air exposure for 5 h and under high‐temperature loading conditions. A failure to form a consistent protective alumina scale or a detrimental shift in mechanical properties would falsify the hypothesis.
